name: Modern liberalism in the United States
summary: American modern liberalism holds that freedom needs economic security as well as freedom from interference, so government should regulate markets and corporations, insure people against want and protect civil rights. It grew out of the Progressive reforms and Wilson's New Freedom, took its form in Roosevelt's New Deal and was given a philosophy by the new liberals.
scope: The mainstream American tradition that the Gale encyclopedia entry on liberalism describes as modern or twentieth-century liberalism: the turn, through the Progressive reforms and Wilson's New Freedom, to Roosevelt's New Deal in 1933, from opposing government in the economy to government as regulator and safety-net, and the new liberal philosophy that the Stanford Encyclopedia says is central to what is called liberalism in American politics. Its own texts here are Roosevelt's Second Bill of Rights message, his fireside chats and speeches of 1934-1941 (the Gale entry names him as the one who introduced it) and Wilson's The New Freedom. It excludes classical liberalism, American libertarianism, the Democratic Party's platforms (a party is not the ideology) and Rawls's liberal egalitarianism as such.

notes: This pass (2026-11-12) rebuilt the audit to rules 7. The earlier answers rested mostly on the Democratic Party's 2024 platform (a party's platform is a coatrack for an ideology) and on Wikipedia, or on the idea that liberals 'would' reject something; those were nulled with their old versions kept in reviewHistory. Defining sources read: Stanford Encyclopedia (Liberalism), the Gale encyclopedia entry, Roosevelt's 1944 message, 1941 Four Freedoms message, 1934-1938 fireside chats and 1936 Madison Square Garden speech, Wilson 1913. Dewey's Liberalism and Social Action and the Stanford entry on his politics were read but not cited: no defining source ties him to this ideology alone (he is also a defining author of pragmatism). Themes searched in them: economy, regulation, unions, taxes, tariffs, property, the state, equality, democracy, violence versus reform, church and state, foreign affairs, civil liberties, ecology. Gender and family, minority and territorial questions, and nationalism have no position in the open texts of Roosevelt, Wilson or the encyclopedias (searched for women, family, minorities, race, immigration, language, secession, patriotism). Most other themes (the criminal law, drugs, guns, migration, abortion, same-sex marriage, the environment, foreign policy, religion, family) have no position in these sources, so they stay null; failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result. Not found: Rawls's own books and the Galbraith and Schlesinger texts were not available as open copies in this pass.
